body:
Craft production in the traditional economy

Crafts have historically been an important part of India's rural and urban economies. Artisans supplied households, farmers, merchants, temples, rulers and travelling traders with a wide range of useful and decorative goods.

As agricultural communities became more settled, the need for specialised occupations increased. Potters made storage vessels, blacksmiths produced implements, carpenters made agricultural and household equipment, and weavers supplied cloth.

A craftsperson was therefore not simply an individual who decorated an object. Craft production involved identifying a need, selecting suitable materials, making the object and ensuring that it could perform its intended function.

Shrenis: historical associations of artisans and traders

In ancient India, groups of artisans and traders sometimes organised themselves into professional associations known as shrenis, or guilds.

Such associations could help regulate aspects of production, maintain professional standards, organise apprenticeship and support economic cooperation among members.

Guilds belonged to particular historical and economic contexts. They should not be confused with modern government departments or treated as identical to present-day craft cooperatives.

The jajmani system

The jajmani system refers to a customary arrangement in which different occupational groups supplied goods or services to patrons and other members of a village community.

Compensation might take the form of grain, other produce or customary benefits instead of a cash payment for every transaction.

For example, a traditional village artisan might supply or repair household implements and receive a share of agricultural produce from the families served.

The system connected artisans to the agricultural economy, but it also operated within an unequal caste-based social structure. Its customary stability should not be interpreted as evidence that all participants had equal freedom, wealth or bargaining power.

Crafts and women's livelihoods

Women have long played important roles in Indian craft production, especially in embroidery, spinning, basketry, textile preparation and several household-based crafts.

Some work was traditionally performed for household use or ceremonial needs, while other products were made for sale.

The distinction between domestic and commercial production matters. A woman who prepares embroidered garments for a family wedding is using a traditional skill for a customary purpose. The same skill can also become a source of income when the work is sold through a craft market or producer organisation.

Greater access to markets can increase economic independence, particularly when artisans have greater control over raw materials, design, pricing and sales.

Trade and the transmission of craft traditions

Indian textiles, metalware, beads and other craft products have participated in regional and long-distance trade for centuries.

Western India, including Gujarat, formed an important textile-producing and trading region. Merchant networks connected production centres to inland markets and maritime trade routes.

Trade did more than transfer finished goods. It also enabled the movement of motifs, materials, techniques and artisans. This helps explain why related forms can appear across adjoining cultural regions, such as Gujarat, Rajasthan and Sindh.

Colonial rule and the pressure of industrial production

Indian handloom production faced serious economic changes during British colonial rule. Industrially produced cloth from British mills competed with handwoven textiles, while colonial economic arrangements encouraged the movement of raw materials and manufactured goods through British-controlled trade networks.

The effects were not uniform for every craft or region. Some specialised luxury goods continued to find patrons, while many traditional producers faced reduced demand or more difficult commercial conditions.

Craft communities also adapted. In colonial Calcutta, for example, Kalighat painters developed single-sheet pictures suited to urban purchasers rather than relying exclusively on older village scroll formats.

Gandhi, khadi and village self-reliance

Mahatma Gandhi connected the revival of spinning and handwoven cloth with the national movement and the economic needs of villages.

In Hind Swaraj (1909) and subsequent writings, he argued for forms of self-reliance that extended beyond political independence.

The charkha, or spinning wheel, became an important symbol of this programme. Hand-spinning could provide supplementary work to rural households, while khadi became associated with swadeshi, self-reliance and resistance to imported industrial cloth.

Gandhi's position was not simply a preference for one fabric over another. It connected the economic condition of ordinary people to larger questions of political independence and the organisation of production.

Modern markets and design change

Many traditional crafts now serve buyers whose needs differ from those of their original communities.

Examples include:

  • A woollen textile traditionally worn by pastoral communities being adapted into a contemporary shawl or home furnishing.
  • Embroidery traditionally used on bridal garments being applied to bags, cushions or wall hangings.
  • Ritual or household painting being produced on paper or canvas for collectors.
  • Traditional metal bells once used with livestock being sold as decorative objects.

Such changes can create additional livelihoods and introduce the craft to new audiences. They may also change the dimensions, materials, colours and customary purposes of the product.

Adaptation is not automatically harmful or beneficial. Its effects depend on whether producers receive reasonable returns, retain meaningful control over their knowledge and can continue transmitting the skills.

Why commercialization does not always benefit artisans

A finished craft object may sell for a high price even when the artisan receives only a small portion of that price.

Possible reasons include costly raw materials, dependence on traders, lack of direct access to customers, transport costs, irregular orders and weak bargaining power.

Traditional artisans may also face competition from machine-made imitations. A cheaper imitation can resemble the original product without involving the same labour or geographical production tradition.

Measures that support continuity

Measures that may help sustain craft livelihoods include access to suitable raw materials, practical training, producer cooperatives, direct marketing opportunities, design development, fair payment and accurate information about the product's origin.

Environmental conditions are also relevant. Crafts that depend on wood, bamboo, natural fibres, metals or clay require reliable access to materials. Unsustainable extraction and pollution can damage both the environment and the livelihood of the artisan.

Preserving a living craft therefore means more than placing old objects in a museum. It also requires conditions under which people can continue to make, use, teach and adapt the craft.

Prelims focus

  • Shreni: historical association or guild of artisans or traders.
  • Jajmani: customary exchange of goods and services between occupational groups and patrons.
  • Colonial industrial production increased competition for traditional Indian handlooms.
  • Hind Swaraj: written by Mahatma Gandhi in 1909.
  • Charkha and khadi: associated with Gandhi's programme of self-reliance and swadeshi.
  • Commercial adaptation can alter a craft's product, material, market and customary use.
  • Trap: A high retail price for a handicraft does not necessarily mean that its artisan receives a high income.

[Sources: NCERT, Craft Traditions of India: Past, Present and Future, Class XII, 'Crafts in the Past', printed pp. 3–10, 'Colonial Rule and Crafts', printed pp. 15–21, and 'Mahatma Gandhi and Self-sufficiency', printed pp. 31–34; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class XI, 'Crafts Heritage', printed pp. 9–14, and 'Painting', printed pp. 107–110; Ministry of Tourism, Incredible India, 'Visit Nirona in Kutch', sections on traditional crafts and changing uses, accessed 23 November 2026.]

title: Artisan Communities, Historical Trade, Livelihoods and Changing Craft Designs

body:
What is a Geographical Indication?

A Geographical Indication (GI) identifies goods that originate from a particular territory, region or locality when a given quality, reputation or other characteristic of the goods is essentially attributable to that geographical origin.

The connection between the product and its place of origin is central. The indication identifies a geographical product tradition rather than merely describing the company that sells an individual article.

For example, Patan Patola is associated with a particular textile-making tradition of Patan. Agates of Cambay identifies a regional stone-working craft associated with Khambhat.

A GI is a legally recognised indication linking goods with their geographical origin and the qualities, reputation or other characteristics associated with that origin.

Legal basis in India

The principal Indian law is the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999. The Act came into force on 15 September 2003.

A GI registration is ordinarily valid for 10 years and can be renewed for further periods of 10 years on application to the Registrar by the registered proprietor or an authorised user and payment of the prescribed fee.

Registration is associated with a defined product and geographical area. Eligible producers within the specified conditions may obtain recognition as authorised users. They apply in writing to the Registrar with supporting documents and the prescribed fee.

A GI should not be confused with a trademark. A trademark generally identifies the commercial source of goods or services, whereas a GI identifies goods whose relevant geographical qualities or reputation are connected with a place.

What GI registration does not mean

A registered GI does not automatically establish that every item sold under a familiar regional name is genuine or that every article from the region meets the registered specifications.

It also does not by itself guarantee that an artisan receives a fair wage, that the product uses only natural materials or that no design changes have occurred.

A traditional art form may exist long before GI registration. The date of registration is therefore not the date on which the art originated.

Registered Gujarat craft indications

The following craft indications appear in the official state-wise GI list with a stated data period of 31 December 2025. The application numbers help identify the exact registry entries, especially where closely related names exist.

Some registered products also have separate logo entries. A product and its registered logo should not automatically be counted as 2 unrelated craft traditions.

Warli Painting: an important geographical exception

Warli Painting is registered under application number 239. Its geographical area is recorded as covering Maharashtra, Gujarat and the relevant neighbouring territories of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.

It therefore illustrates why a geographical indication may cover an area extending across modern state boundaries. The principal cultural association with Maharashtra does not mean that Gujarat is excluded from the registered geographical area.

Application date and certificate date are not identical

GI records commonly contain several different dates, including the application filing date and the date of the registration certificate.

For example:

  • Patan Patola, application 232: filed on 9 March 2011; the individual registry record shows a certificate dated 9 September 2013.
  • Kutch Ajrakh Print of Gujarat, application 1050: filed on 31 January 2023; the registry's document list records a registration certificate dated 22 April 2024.
  • Bharuch Sujani Weaving, application 1090: filed on 22 May 2023; the registry shows a certificate dated 30 March 2024.

The date-of-filing column in the state-wise list must therefore not be interpreted as the date of GI certification.

The state-wise list used here reports registrations as of 31 December 2025 and was consulted on 23 November 2026. These are different dates. The examples establish registered status within that stated data period; the list is not represented as a newly compiled November 2026 register.

How GI recognition can support livelihoods

A GI can help buyers identify a product's regional origin and distinguish it from goods that improperly use the protected indication.

For artisans, this may support product recognition, marketing and preservation of specialised geographical traditions. However, the benefit depends on practical conditions such as authorised-user participation, enforcement, producer organisation, buyer awareness and fair commercial arrangements.

Legal recognition and economic success are therefore connected but distinct.

Prelims focus

  • GI law: Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999.
  • Commencement of the Act: 15 September 2003.
  • Ordinary GI registration period: 10 years, renewable.
  • Patan Patola and Rajkot Patola have separate GI registrations.
  • Jamnagari Bandhani and Kutch Bandhani have separate GI registrations.
  • Warli Painting has a registered geographical area extending beyond Maharashtra.
  • Trap: A GI application filing date is not necessarily the registration certificate date.

[Sources: Intellectual Property India, 'Geographical Indications: An Introduction', and 'Geographical Indications Act', official GI information pages, accessed 23 November 2026; Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999; Intellectual Property India, 'State wise Registered GI of India', 'Details of GI Applications Registered as on December 31, 2025', Gujarat entries and the multi-state Warli Painting entry, accessed 23 November 2026; Intellectual Property India, GI public-search application details for Patan Patola, application 232; Kutch Ajrakh Print of Gujarat, application 1050; and Bharuch Sujani Weaving, application 1090, accessed 23 November 2026.]
